newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian republican movement around since 1788.
newsitem.headline: Australian republican movement around since 1788.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard's decision to seek party approval for a possible vote on whether the nation becomes a republic is an idea that has been around since the first white settlers arrived in 1788.
Early settlers, many of them Irish, believed a colony was a temporary stage of political development, with separation from Britain and a republic the inevitable outcome.
They looked frequently to the United States, which severed ties with Britian and became a republic, as an example of what Australia might become.

Dissatisfaction with British rule came to a head in October 1854 when Irish gold miners, protesting police oppression and taxes, began an armed rebellion and raised a new Australian flag at the Eureka stockade near Ballarat in Victoria state.
The rebellion, which rallied under a blue flag emblazoned with white Southern Cross stars, was crushed, but became widely regarded as the birthplace of Australian republicanism.
Colonial self-government was granted in 1856 and more Australians began to regard getting rid of monarchical connections as an essential part of a maturing society.

In 1887, the Bulletin newspaper published a poem by Henry Lawson "A Song of the Republic". In it, Lawson called for the "Sons of the South" to choose between "The Land that belongs to the Lord and Queen, or the Land that belongs to you".

But after federation in 1901, which established Australia as a nation with its own parliament but with allegiance to Britain's monarchy, and through the first half of this century, the republican debate remained on the political fringe.

Ties to Britian began to weaken after World War Two when Australia looked toward the United States for defence and cultural ties. Massive immigration programmes after the war and a new multiculturalism also began to dilute Australian sentiment towards Britain.

On November 11, 1975, Labor prime minister Gough Whitlam, an avowed republican, was dismissed by the Queen's representative in Australia, governor-general Sir John Kerr, due to the upper house's refusal to pass a finance bill.

Whitlam had previously changed Australia's national anthem from God Save the Queen to Advance Australia Fair, and removed references to the monarchy in Australia's oath of allegiance in its citizenship ceremony.

But it was Whitlam's controversial dismissal that reignited the republican debate, polarising it along political lines for the first time. Labor supported republicanism, while the conservative Liberals remained staunch monarchists.
Yet for much of the 1980s and early 1990s, the issue disappeared from the public and political arena. In 1991, the Australian Republican Movement was formed to stir debate.
Labor prime minister Paul Keating ignited the debate in 1995 when he declared his intention to move Australia toward a republic by the turn of the century.
"It is the government's view that Australia's head-of-state should be an Australian -- that Australia should become a republic by the year 2001," Keating told parliament.
"Australia's head-of-state should embody and represent Australian views and traditions, Australian experience and aspirations."
Keating called for a nationwide vote on the issue before the turn of the century, later saying a republic would enhance Australia's standing in the booming Asia-Pacific region.
His stance divided the nation. But in recent years, opinion polls have shown that more than half of Australians now favour a republic -- at issue is how to create it.
Pro-republican politicans favour a minimalist approach where a president appointed by two-thirds of both houses of parliament would assume the role of the current governor-general.
But many Australians want a popularly elected president, as in France, something the politicans fear would give the president more power than the parliament.
Monarchist prime minister Howard, elected in March 1996, has pledged to hold a public convention to debate the issue, with a possible nationwide vote before 2000.
